paragraphs: A generative model can assign an unfamiliar example a higher likelihood than familiar training data, yet almost never produce examples like it. This paper explains how those two observations can coexist. The central distinction is between probability density at a location and the total probability mass contained in the surrounding region.

A region can have high density but occupy so little space that its total probability mass remains small. The authors show how this situation can arise near data concentrated on low-dimensional manifolds: structures with fewer effective dimensions than the space containing them. This geometry helps explain why a high likelihood need not imply that a sample belongs to the distribution the model usually generates.

The proposed detector combines likelihood with an estimate of local intrinsic dimension from a pretrained generative model. It applies to normalizing flows and score-based diffusion models. On the reported benchmarks, this combination matches or exceeds leading detection methods using the same model backbones, supporting the value of interpreting likelihood alongside local geometry.
icml-2024-a-geometric-explanation-of-the.tldr: Combining likelihood with local dimensionality helps explain and detect unfamiliar data that generative models misleadingly score highly.

paragraphs: A classifier's confidence is useful only when it reflects how often its predictions are correct. Large neural networks can classify images accurately while reporting poorly calibrated confidence. This paper investigates whether changing how different parts of the network are trained can improve that alignment while preserving classification accuracy.

The authors separate training of the feature extraction layers from training of the classification layers. These components serve different roles: one builds representations of the input, while the other converts those representations into predictions. Decoupling their training improves calibration in the studied over-parameterized architectures, with low training cost and retained accuracy.

A further modification places a Gaussian prior on the outputs of the last hidden layer and uses variational training during the classification stage. This produces additional calibration improvements. Experiments cover Vision Transformers and Wide Residual Networks on several image classification benchmarks. The findings indicate that training organization, together with probabilistic treatment of the final representation, can improve confidence estimates without requiring an observed accuracy tradeoff in these evaluations.
icml-2024-decoupling-feature-extraction-.tldr: Training feature extraction and classification separately improves neural-network calibration while retaining accuracy in the reported image experiments.

paragraphs: Video super-resolution aims to recover detailed, higher-resolution video from lower-resolution inputs. Event signals offer finely timed information that has previously been used to improve motion estimation and alignment between frames. EvTexture explores another use for this information: recovering the fine textures that make image regions look detailed.

The method adds a dedicated texture enhancement branch that draws on high-frequency details in the events. An iterative module progressively uses their high temporal resolution to restore texture. Instead of obtaining all of the refinement in a single step, the model revisits texture regions across multiple iterations, gradually improving the reconstructed details.

The authors report leading performance on four datasets. On Vid4, which contains rich textures, the improvement over recent event-based methods reaches up to 4.67 dB. That maximum is specific to the stated comparison, rather than an improvement promised for every video. The results support treating events as a source of appearance detail as well as a tool for tracking movement, broadening their role in video reconstruction.
icml-2024-evtexture-event-driven-texture.tldr: EvTexture progressively uses event signals to restore fine textures, achieving leading video super-resolution results on four datasets.

paragraphs: Uncertain predictions can reflect randomness in the world or gaps in a model's understanding. Those two causes require different interpretations, but ordinary probabilistic predictions do not separate them. This paper develops a way to estimate the knowledge gaps, including situations where existing uncertainty methods become overconfident because a model underfits.

The training strategy uses pairs of independent responses drawn from the true distribution for the same input. The model predicts the pair and is also allowed to see one response while predicting the other. Measuring how much this extra information improves prediction provides a signal about what the model has not learned about the underlying process.

The authors prove that using this opportunity whenever it helps is equivalent to second-order calibration. This property supports provably correct frequentist confidence intervals for the true conditional distribution and high-probability detection of incorrect responses. Experiments on ambiguous image classification, synthetic language modeling, and partially observable navigation show more accurate estimates of missing knowledge than existing techniques. The theoretical guarantee concerns the stated calibration property, rather than every model trained with paired examples.
icml-2024-experts-dont-cheat-learning-wh.tldr: Predicting paired responses and measuring the benefit of seeing one helps models quantify gaps in their knowledge.

paragraphs: Some data naturally occupy curved spaces, so generating realistic samples requires respecting that geometry. Existing manifold-based generative methods can involve expensive divergence calculations or approximations of heat kernels. These requirements make complicated geometries and high-dimensional problems difficult to handle. This paper introduces Riemannian Diffusion Mixture to address those obstacles.

The framework constructs a generative process by combining bridge processes defined on general manifolds. These bridges guide the evolving sample toward data points without requiring heat-kernel estimates. The authors derive a geometric interpretation of the resulting drift: it is a weighted average of tangent directions toward the data. This describes how the process moves toward the target distribution while accounting for the surrounding geometry.

The paper also develops a scalable training objective for learning this mixture process on general manifolds. Reported experiments show superior performance across diverse manifolds while substantially reducing the number of simulation steps used during training. The contribution therefore links an interpretable geometric construction with a training procedure intended to make manifold generation more computationally practical.
icml-2024-generative-modeling-on-manifol.tldr: A mixture of geometric bridge processes enables manifold-aware generation without heat-kernel estimation and with fewer training simulation steps.

paragraphs: Generating a graph requires getting its pattern of connections right, alongside any attributes attached to its components. The paper argues that learning to remove noise does not explicitly teach a diffusion model the final graph structure it should produce. Its proposed framework makes that final structure a direct learning target.

The generative process mixes diffusion processes conditioned on their endpoints. A predicted final graph guides the evolving sample, which the authors report leads to rapid convergence. They also introduce a simple parameterization and an objective for learning the endpoint structure that enables maximum likelihood training. This connects the model's training target to the topology sought at the end of generation.

Experiments cover general graphs and both two-dimensional and three-dimensional molecular generation. The authors report improvements over previous generative models, including graphs with correct topology and combinations of discrete attributes, such as atom types, and continuous attributes, such as spatial coordinates. These findings support explicitly predicting the destination graph as a useful way to coordinate structural and attribute generation.
icml-2024-graph-generation-with-diffusio.tldr: Predicting final graph structures guides a diffusion mixture toward better graph and molecule generation in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Graph classification assigns a category to an entire graph. HEAL addresses settings with few labeled graphs and many unlabeled ones, where effective use of the available structure matters especially strongly. The paper also targets the difficulty of representing relationships that involve groups of nodes beyond ordinary pairwise connections.

Its first branch learns a hypergraph structure adaptively. Hyperedges represent relationships among groups of nodes, allowing the model to explore more complex dependencies. A second branch builds a line graph from the learned hypergraph to represent interactions between those hyperedges. Together, the branches examine relationships within node groups and relationships between the groups themselves.

Relational consistency learning connects the two branches so they can transfer knowledge and guide one another. This makes their distinct structural views part of a shared learning framework for semi-supervised classification. Experiments on real-world graph datasets support HEAL's effectiveness against existing leading methods. The reported contribution combines richer structural representations with a mechanism for coordinating them when labeled examples are scarce.
icml-2024-hypergraph-enhanced-dual-semi-.tldr: HEAL combines learned hypergraphs and interactions between hyperedges to improve graph classification with limited labels.

paragraphs: A useful uncertainty estimate should distinguish unpredictable outcomes from uncertainty caused by limited model knowledge. Evidential deep learning attempts to represent these distinctions by predicting second-order distributions: probability distributions over possible predictive distributions. This paper examines whether the resulting quantities can be interpreted faithfully as uncertainty about what a model knows.

The authors analyze the learning objectives used to fit these richer distributions. Their framework covers classification, regression, and count prediction, allowing them to investigate issues shared across a wide range of approaches. Two central concerns are identifiability, or whether the learning problem determines the intended uncertainty representation, and convergence, or what minimizing the objective actually leads toward.

The analysis also highlights that the resulting measures of epistemic uncertainty have a relative rather than absolute character. This matters because a numerical uncertainty output can appear more definitive than its training objective justifies. The paper's contribution is a theoretical account of difficulties in optimization and interpretation, helping clarify what these methods' uncertainty estimates can mean rather than treating the presence of a second-order distribution as sufficient assurance.
icml-2024-is-epistemic-uncertainty-faith.tldr: The paper identifies theoretical difficulties in learning and interpreting epistemic uncertainty through evidential deep learning.

paragraphs: When a model moves to a different data distribution, its confidence and its relative standing against other models can become unreliable. Unsupervised domain adaptation makes this especially difficult because the target domain has no labels. This paper addresses both confidence calibration and model selection through a shared question: how accurately does the model perform on groups of examples?

The proposed method estimates group accuracy using importance weights. These weights account for distribution differences when forming the estimate. The authors formulate an optimization problem to find weights that produce accurate group accuracy estimates and provide theoretical analysis of that formulation. Group accuracy thus becomes the common quantity supporting two otherwise distinct evaluation tasks.

In extensive experiments, the authors report improvements over state-of-the-art performance of 22% for calibration and 14% for model selection. These are the improvements stated for the evaluated tasks, rather than percentage-point gains in classification accuracy. The results suggest that better estimation of group-level correctness can help both adjust confidence and choose models under distribution shift without target labels.
icml-2024-iw-gae-importance-weighted-gro.tldr: Importance-weighted estimates of group accuracy improve calibration and model selection when target-domain labels are unavailable.

paragraphs: Coverage path planning asks an agent to traverse all accessible space within an area. When the environment is unknown, the agent must decide where to move while simultaneously discovering the map. This makes the problem different from computing a fixed route over a fully known layout, with applications including robotic mowing and search-and-rescue.

The paper studies how reinforcement learning can handle this setting by examining several connected design choices: the available actions, the information shown to the model, its neural architecture, and its reward. It proposes a computationally feasible map representation organized around the agent and based on frontiers, which mark boundaries relevant to further exploration.

The authors also introduce a reward term based on total variation to encourage complete coverage. The representation and reward address complementary needs: making the evolving environment manageable for the learner and guiding it toward the coverage objective. Extensive experiments across multiple coverage-planning variations show performance exceeding earlier reinforcement-learning approaches and highly specialized methods, supporting the effectiveness of the combined design.
icml-2024-learning-coverage-paths-in-unk.tldr: An agent-centered frontier map and a coverage-promoting reward improve learned routes through unknown environments.

paragraphs: Algorithmic recourse seeks an executable change that turns an unfavorable model prediction into a favorable one while keeping the required effort reasonable. Such a change may not exist when a classifier is trained solely for predictive performance. This paper incorporates the availability of recourse into the process of learning tree-based models.

The authors formulate tree learning as an accuracy-focused task constrained to make reasonable actions available for as many instances as possible. They propose an efficient greedy algorithm that builds the tree from the top down using techniques from adversarial training. They also show how the approach can be applied to random forests, extending it from individual trees to ensembles.

Experiments find that the learned models provide reasonable actions for more instances than the baselines, without significantly reducing accuracy or computational efficiency. The goal is broader access to recourse, rather than a claim that every individual necessarily receives an action. The findings support considering the possibility of changing an outcome during model construction, when the decision rules themselves can still be shaped.
icml-2024-learning-decision-trees-and-fo.tldr: Training trees with recourse constraints makes reasonable prediction-changing actions available to more instances while largely preserving accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: A visual concept can include examples that share an underlying organization while differing in their details. This paper studies how to capture that shared organization in a program inferred from a small set of examples. Its neurosymbolic approach combines learned inference with explicit programmatic representations of visual structure.

The proposed Template Programs use expressions from a domain-specific language to describe structural and parameter patterns common to a concept. The authors develop a learning procedure that trains networks to infer these programs directly from visual datasets organized into concept groups. The resulting representation supports multiple tasks, including generating examples from limited input and parsing related examples to identify corresponding segments.

Experiments span two-dimensional layouts, Omniglot characters, and three-dimensional shapes. The method outperforms task-specific alternatives and is competitive with domain-specific approaches in the limited domains where those approaches exist. These findings support template programs as a reusable representation across visual tasks and domains, with shared structure serving both the interpretation of existing examples and the generation of new ones.
icml-2024-learning-to-infer-generative-t.tldr: Learned template programs capture shared visual structure to support generation and segmentation across several visual domains.

paragraphs: A vision-language model may describe the same three-dimensional object differently from different viewpoints. Combining those descriptions using a language model can introduce hallucinations when the descriptions conflict. This paper proposes combining probabilistic evidence from the views to make large-scale object annotation more reliable.

The method uses the vision-language model's joint image-text likelihoods and aggregates over factors such as viewpoint. This provides an alternative to merging independently generated text descriptions. The authors report improved reliability and efficiency, together with leading object-type inference performance measured against human-verified labels. The aggregation therefore addresses both inconsistent descriptions and the accuracy of the final annotation.

The annotations also help conditional prediction: supplying an object's type as auxiliary text improves downstream predictions such as material identification. Such inputs additionally let the authors investigate the contribution of visual information compared with reasoning from text alone in an unsupervised setting. Across supervised and unsupervised evaluations, the paper demonstrates a pipeline producing reliable annotations for 764,000 Objaverse objects, connecting its aggregation method to annotation at substantial scale.
icml-2024-leveraging-vlm-based-pipelines.tldr: Aggregating image-text likelihoods across viewpoints improves the reliability and efficiency of large-scale 3D object annotation.

paragraphs: Minimum Bayes Risk decoding chooses a generated text candidate by evaluating its expected risk under a probability model and a chosen utility function. Computing this expectation over every possible text is impractical, so the decision usually relies on a sampled collection of candidates. The paper examines how probabilities are assigned within that approximation.

Common implementations make two approximations: restricting the calculation to sampled texts and estimating their probabilities through Monte Carlo sampling. The authors retain the sampled collection but replace the Monte Carlo probability estimate with probabilities obtained directly from the generation model. Their argument is that this second approximation is avoidable when model probabilities are available during inference.

The resulting method, model-based MBR, changes how existing candidates contribute to the decision without requiring enumeration of all possible texts. Analytical and empirical results favor its probability estimate over the Monte Carlo alternative. Experiments report better performance than conventional MBR on several text generation tasks using both encoder-decoder models and language models, showing that the choice of probability estimator can materially affect decoding quality.
icml-2024-model-based-minimum-bayes-risk.tldr: Using model probabilities directly improves minimum Bayes Risk decoding over Monte Carlo probability estimates in several text generation tasks.

paragraphs: Speech combines several attributes at once: linguistic content, prosody, vocal timbre, and acoustic detail. NaturalSpeech 3 addresses the difficulty of generating this mixture by separating those attributes into different representational spaces. The system uses that factorization to support natural speech synthesis in a zero-shot setting.

Its neural codec applies factorized vector quantization to represent the waveform through separate subspaces for the different speech attributes. A factorized diffusion model then generates the attributes in their respective spaces, guided by the corresponding prompts. This divides a complicated generation problem into parts while keeping the representation organized around properties that matter for the resulting speech.

The authors report that this design models speech effectively and efficiently. In their experiments, NaturalSpeech 3 outperforms leading text-to-speech systems on quality, similarity, prosody, and intelligibility. These results span both how the generated voice sounds and how clearly it communicates the intended content. The paper's central contribution is the coordinated use of factorization in the speech codec and the generative model, so that both stages work with the same separation of attributes.
icml-2024-naturalspeech-3-zero-shot-spee.tldr: NaturalSpeech 3 separates speech attributes in its codec and diffusion models, improving zero-shot speech synthesis in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Sequential decision-making requires balancing promising actions with exploration, and that balance depends on how noisy observations are. A conservatively specified noise level can make uncertainty estimates unnecessarily broad. This paper develops confidence sets for linear bandits that adapt more closely to the noise actually present.

The first construction is semi-adaptive: its normalized width scales with the square root of the dimension times the true sub-Gaussian noise parameter, plus the specified parameter. The standard comparison instead multiplies the specified parameter by the dimension. The improvement is especially relevant in high dimensions when the specified noise level is much larger than the true one, and it yields an improved regret bound.

For bounded rewards, the authors also develop a variance-adaptive confidence set and an optimistic bandit algorithm with a new regret analysis. Both constructions rely on an online-learning regret equality. The bounded-reward construction shows substantially improved numerical performance over prior approaches. Evaluations on Bayesian optimization tasks find better or comparable performance to existing methods, connecting the confidence-set analysis to practical sequential optimization.
icml-2024-noise-adaptive-confidence-sets.tldr: Noise-adaptive confidence sets improve linear-bandit guarantees and deliver better or comparable Bayesian optimization performance.

paragraphs: Self-attention becomes expensive on long sequences because its time and memory costs grow quadratically with sequence length. This paper explores replacing softmax attention with high-degree polynomial attention. The authors first demonstrate that this replacement can preserve model quality, establishing a basis for a more computationally efficient attention mechanism.

They then use polynomial sketching techniques from numerical linear algebra to approximate the new attention calculation in linear time, with approximation guarantees. The approach does not require making attention matrices sparse. A separate block-based algorithm handles causal masking efficiently, allowing the architecture to respect the ordering constraints needed for language modeling.

The resulting PolySketchFormer is evaluated on synthetic data and on PG19, Wikipedia, and C4 using Google Cloud TPUs. For GPT-2-style models with 32,000-token contexts, the authors report twice the training speed of the fastest FlashAttention configuration, with no observed quality degradation across their experiments. This is a demonstrated result for the tested settings; the broader contribution is an attention replacement whose efficient approximation has theoretical support.
icml-2024-polysketchformer-fast-transfor.tldr: PolySketchFormer uses sketched polynomial attention for linear-time computation, achieving twice the training speed in a reported long-context comparison.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning research often evaluates a new algorithm by comparing its performance with standard algorithms on benchmark environments. This position paper questions how much that practice can reliably establish under realistic computational constraints. Its concern is that experiments continue to support misleading or insufficiently justified claims despite repeated calls for better evaluation.

The authors investigate why rigorous experimental designs require more computation. Their argument connects the quality of the evidence to the resources needed to obtain it: making benchmark comparisons reliable can demand substantial computational time. They conclude that the costs of rigorous performance benchmarking are likely to be prohibitive in many cases.

The paper therefore advocates an additional experimentation paradigm to complement benchmarking. It presents a methodological argument about how research evidence is produced, rather than a new reinforcement-learning algorithm. Its implication is that improving scientific practice requires considering whether the desired experiment is computationally feasible, alongside whether it is rigorous. Benchmark results remain part of the research process, but the authors argue that additional forms of experimentation are needed to address their limitations.
icml-2024-position-benchmarking-is-limit.tldr: The authors argue that rigorous reinforcement-learning benchmarking is often prohibitively costly and should be complemented by another experimentation paradigm.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that autoregressive language models cannot independently perform planning or verify their own reasoning. At the same time, the authors see substantial value in their broad, approximate knowledge. Their proposal is to organize planning systems so that language models contribute that knowledge while external components perform model-based verification.

The proposed LLM-Modulo framework uses close, two-way interaction between language models and external verifiers. The language model has a broader role than translating inputs or formatting outputs: it can also help acquire the models that drive verification. This makes its knowledge useful in constructing the formal machinery used to assess planning and reasoning.

The authors argue that this interaction offers a stronger integration of neural and symbolic components than a simple sequential pipeline. They also envision extending model-based planning to accommodate more flexible knowledge, problem descriptions, and preferences. These are the paper's position and proposed direction, rather than a universal empirical performance result. The central architectural idea is to connect approximate knowledge generation with external checking throughout the planning process.
icml-2024-position-llms-cant-plan-but-ca.tldr: The authors advocate tightly coupling LLM knowledge with external model-based verification to support planning and reasoning.

paragraphs: Neural Radiance Fields learn a three-dimensional scene from images, but temporary objects can interfere with that reconstruction. A pedestrian or bird may appear in only some views, making the training images inconsistent. PruNeRF identifies and removes such distracting content without requiring advance knowledge of the distractors' types and quantities.

The method begins with pixel-level measurements of distraction, introducing influence functions to improve their accuracy. It then uses depth-based reprojection to assess consistency in three-dimensional space. This adds information about how observations relate across views, producing distraction estimates that account for the scene's geometry rather than treating pixels independently.

Finally, segmentation refines those pixel-level estimates into decisions about image regions. The combination of influence measurements, geometric consistency, and segment-level refinement is designed to identify distractors more precisely. On benchmark datasets, the authors report consistently greater robustness to distractors than existing leading methods. The contribution is a dataset-pruning framework that uses the shared three-dimensional scene to guide which training content should be excluded.
icml-2024-prunerf-segment-centric-datase.tldr: PruNeRF combines influence measurements, 3D consistency, and segmentation to remove distracting training content and improve scene reconstruction robustness.

paragraphs: The paper studies replicable learning of large-margin halfspaces, a setting involving linear decision boundaries with a margin. It develops algorithms that improve the amount of training data required while examining how those improvements interact with computational cost. The results distinguish efficient learning from alternatives that spend considerably more time to reduce sample requirements.

The first algorithm runs in polynomial time, is dimension-independent, and is proper, meaning it returns a hypothesis from the class being learned. Its sample complexity improves on the cited earlier replicable algorithms across all relevant parameters. Its dependence on the accuracy parameter is also optimal.

The authors then explore two more computationally expensive constructions. A reduction from differential privacy to replicability improves dependence on the margin but requires doubly exponential time in the inverse squared margin and worsens accuracy dependence relative to the first algorithm. Their final construction improves sample complexity over both earlier constructions and needs exponential time in the inverse squared margin. Together, these results sharpen the available tradeoffs between data requirements and computation for replicable learning.
icml-2024-replicable-learning-of-large-m.tldr: New replicable halfspace learners improve sample complexity, with distinct tradeoffs between polynomial-time efficiency and more data-efficient exponential-time algorithms.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search becomes cheaper when promising networks can be identified before investing in full training. Many performance predictors nevertheless need training data consisting of networks that have already been trained. Zero-cost proxies reduce this expense, but the paper notes that they can be biased by network properties and offer limited predictive performance.

The authors propose neural graph features, called GRAF, which are simple properties computed from a network's architectural graph. These features provide an interpretable description of architecture for performance prediction. The approach investigates how much useful predictive information is available directly in network structure, without relying solely on existing zero-cost signals.

GRAF delivers fast performance prediction and outperforms zero-cost proxies and other common architectural encodings in the reported comparisons. When combined with other zero-cost proxies, it exceeds most existing performance predictors at a fraction of their cost. This distinction matters: the strongest stated comparison concerns the combined approach. The findings show that inexpensive, interpretable structural features can make a substantial contribution to predicting which architectures will perform well.
icml-2024-surprisingly-strong-performanc.tldr: Simple architectural graph features provide strong, inexpensive performance prediction, especially when combined with zero-cost proxies.

paragraphs: Transferring a visual classifier to a new domain is difficult when the target data look different and lack labels. LaGTran uses text descriptions to help move discriminative knowledge across that gap. The approach is motivated by the authors' observation that semantically rich text has more favorable transfer properties than working exclusively with visual appearance.

The framework trains a text classifier on the source domain, then applies it to descriptions of target-domain examples. Those predictions become supervision for the corresponding target images. Language therefore provides an intermediate route for transferring class information from labeled source data to unlabeled visual data in a different domain.

The authors report substantial improvements over prior approaches on challenging image datasets including GeoNet and DomainNet. They also introduce Ego2Exo, a benchmark for transferring between egocentric and exocentric video views, and find significant gains there. These results extend the method's evaluated scope beyond images. The contribution is a simple transfer mechanism in which predictions from text supply training guidance for visual recognition under substantial domain differences.
icml-2024-tell-dont-show-language-guidan.tldr: LaGTran uses predictions from text descriptions to supervise visual domain adaptation, improving transfer across tested image and video domains.

paragraphs: Few-shot node classification asks a model to classify graph nodes from very few labeled examples. Training graph meta-learning methods for this task can itself be constrained by scarce labels. Neighbors as Queries, or NaQ, constructs training episodes without labels so that information from all graph nodes can be used.

Each episode begins by randomly sampling nodes to form a support set. The method then samples similar nodes to form the corresponding query set. This creates a training structure that resembles the downstream few-shot task. The authors contrast that task-aware organization with unsupervised graph contrastive learning, which can overlook the downstream format and become vulnerable to class imbalance.

NaQ is model-agnostic, allowing existing supervised graph meta-learning methods to be trained through unsupervised episodes. The authors report little performance loss in some cases and improvements in others, alongside extensive experiments supporting the method's effectiveness. The contribution is an episode-generation procedure rather than a particular prediction architecture, making the training examples' organization the mechanism for using unlabeled graph information.
icml-2024-unsupervised-episode-generatio.tldr: NaQ builds label-free training episodes from sampled nodes and similar neighbors to support few-shot graph node classification.

paragraphs: Watermarks in language-model output are intended to help identify AI-generated text. This paper challenges claims that current schemes are ready for deployment by studying watermark stealing: approximately learning a watermark through queries to the API of a watermarked model. The authors identify this as a vulnerability in the schemes they examine.

The study considers two consequences. Spoofing makes text appear to carry the watermark, while scrubbing removes evidence of the watermark from generated text. The authors show that stealing a watermark enables practical spoofing and also substantially improves scrubbing. They introduce an automated watermark-stealing algorithm and evaluate both attack types in realistic settings.

For the evaluated state-of-the-art schemes, the authors report that an attacker can carry out spoofing and scrubbing for under $50, with average success exceeding 80%. These findings concern the tested schemes and conditions, rather than proving every possible watermark ineffective. They nevertheless weaken deployment-readiness claims for schemes previously considered safe and motivate watermark designs that remain robust when their behavior can be approximately inferred.
icml-2024-watermark-stealing-in-large-la.tldr: Approximately learning an LLM watermark enables low-cost spoofing and scrubbing with high average success against the evaluated schemes.
